_comment: Hand-written coursework, one lesson per unit, keyed by unit id from units.json. Deliberately not model-generated: a beginner's first contact with a language should be the same every time, correct, and free of quota. Step types: 'sounds' (pronunciation), 'words' (vocabulary, each spoken), 'grammar' (explained in English with examples and an optional table), 'check' (one question, graded on the device). Keep every explanation shorter than it wants to be. Text may use the persona placeholders of units.json ({{name}}, {{role_de}}, {{he}}, …); app.services.curriculum.lesson_for_user renders them for whoever is logged in, so never write a learner's name here.

a1.1-1.title: Hallo und Tschüss
a1.1-1.intro: Your first German. By the end of this lesson you can greet someone, say your name, say where you are from, and ask someone the same back. Nothing here assumes you have seen German before.

steps.title: Five sounds, then you can read almost anything
steps.body: German spelling is honest: a letter almost always sounds the same way. Five rules cover most of it, and you can come back to this page any time.
steps.note: So 'wie' is said 'vee', and 'Wien' is 'veen'. The two dots in ä, ö, ü change the vowel — you will pick them up by ear, and the tutor will say them for you as often as you like.

steps.title: Hello and goodbye
steps.body: German separates the time of day. Nobody will mind if you get it wrong, but these four will cover your whole day.

items.note: safe at any time, with anyone
the normal daytime greeting; there is no German 'good afternoon'
formal; in a shop or an office

steps.title: du and Sie — the one choice you make constantly
steps.body: German has two words for 'you'. 'du' is for friends, family, children and most colleagues. 'Sie' is for strangers, officials, shopkeepers, your landlord and anyone much older. Sie is always written with a capital S. Getting it wrong is a small thing — Germans will often invite you to switch with 'Wir können uns duzen' — but using Sie first is never rude.

examples.de: Wie heißt du?
examples.en: What's your name?

examples.de: Wie heißen Sie?
examples.en: What's your name?

examples.de: Woher kommst du?
examples.en: Where are you from?

steps.note: Colleagues in German tech teams are usually du, and so are fellow students at a German university. The Ausländerbehörde is definitely Sie.

steps.question: Your new landlord, a man of about sixty, says 'Guten Tag'. You want to ask his name. What do you say?
options: Wie heißt du?
Wie heißen Sie?
Wie heißt Sie?
steps.why: A landlord is Sie. With Sie the verb ends in -en: heißen, kommen, wohnen. 'Wie heißt du?' is for a colleague or a friend.

steps.title: ich bin — I am
steps.body: 'sein' means 'to be'. It is irregular in every language and German is no exception, so learn these as whole words rather than as a rule. These four cover nearly everything you need at the start.

examples.de: Ich bin {{name}}.
examples.en: I am {{name}}.

examples.de: Ich bin aus Jordanien.
examples.en: I am from Jordan.

examples.de: Sie sind Frau Keller?
examples.en: You are Mrs Keller?

examples.de: Sie ist aus Hamburg.
examples.en: She is from Hamburg.

steps.note: sie with a small s means 'she'. Sie with a capital S is the polite 'you'. Spoken, they sound the same, so listen to the verb: sie ist (she is), Sie sind (you are).

steps.question: You meet your new neighbour. How do you say 'I am {{name}}'?
options: Ich bin {{name}}.
Du bist {{name}}.
Ich ist {{name}}.
steps.why: 'ich' always goes with 'bin'. 'du bist' would be telling her that she is {{name}}.

steps.title: Saying who you are
steps.body: Two ways to give your name. 'Ich heiße' is the more German-sounding one, and it is what you will hear back.

items.note: German has no separate 'am learning' — one form does both

steps.title: Asking back: the W-questions
steps.body: German question words mostly start with W, and the verb comes straight after them. Learn the question and its answer together — that pairing is what makes a conversation possible.
steps.note: woher = where from, wo = where. One letter, and it is the difference between your country and your street.

examples.de: Woher kommen Sie?
examples.en: Where are you from?
examples.note: to a stranger: Sie, and the verb ends in -en

examples.de: Wo wohnst du?
examples.en: Where do you live?

examples.de: Was machst du in Amman?
examples.en: What do you do in Amman?

steps.question: Someone asks 'Woher kommst du?'. What are they asking?
options: Where do you live?
Where are you from?
What is your name?
steps.why: woher = where from. 'Wo wohnst du?' would be where you live.

steps.title: Numbers 0 to 12
steps.body: You need these for times, prices and your phone number. Say them out loud — the tutor will ask you for them later.
steps.note: On the phone Germans often say 'zwo' instead of 'zwei', so it cannot be confused with 'drei'.

steps.title: The verb comes second. Always.
steps.body: This is the one rule that makes German sound German. In a normal statement the verb is the second thing in the sentence — not necessarily the second word, but the second block. Whatever you put first, the verb follows it immediately, and the subject moves behind the verb.

examples.de: Ich wohne in Amman.
examples.en: I live in Amman.

examples.de: In Amman wohne ich.
examples.en: In Amman I live.
examples.note: put the place first and 'ich' moves behind the verb

examples.de: Heute arbeite ich zu Hause.
examples.en: Today I work at home.

steps.note: This will be your most common mistake for months, and the tutor will keep catching it. That is normal and it is not a sign you are bad at this.

steps.question: Which one is correct German?
options: Heute ich arbeite zu Hause.
Heute arbeite ich zu Hause.
Arbeite heute ich zu Hause.
steps.why: 'Heute' takes the first slot, so the verb 'arbeite' must come second and 'ich' goes after it.

steps.title: When you are stuck
steps.body: The most useful sentences in the language. Learn these before anything else and you can survive any conversation.

items.note: this one buys you enormous patience

steps.title: On the stairs
steps.body: Frau Keller meets her new neighbour, Samir, on the stairs. You will hear it first, then read it. Listen for two things: where Samir comes from, and what he says when he does not catch a question.

lines.de: Guten Tag! Ich bin Frau Keller. Wie heißen Sie?
lines.en: Hello! I'm Mrs Keller. What's your name?

lines.de: Guten Tag! Ich heiße Samir Haddad.
lines.en: Hello! My name is Samir Haddad.

lines.de: Woher kommen Sie, Herr Haddad?
lines.en: Where are you from, Mr Haddad?

lines.de: Wie bitte? Langsamer, bitte.
lines.en: Sorry? Slower, please.

lines.de: Woher kommen Sie?
lines.en: Where are you from?

lines.de: Ich komme aus Jordanien, aus Amman. Und Sie?
lines.en: I come from Jordan, from Amman. And you?

lines.de: Ich komme aus Hamburg.
lines.en: I come from Hamburg.

steps.question: Where does Samir come from?
options: From Hamburg
From Amman, in Jordan
From Berlin
steps.why: 'Ich komme aus Jordanien, aus Amman.' Hamburg is where Frau Keller comes from: Samir's 'Und Sie?' turned the question back to her.

steps.question: Samir did not catch the question. What did he say?
options: Wie bitte? Langsamer, bitte.
Wie heißen Sie? Und Sie?
Ich lerne Deutsch. Tschüss!
steps.why: 'Wie bitte?' is the polite 'sorry, what?', and 'Langsamer, bitte' asks for it slower. Germans will happily repeat: these two lines keep any conversation going.

a1.1-1.outro: That is everything you need to introduce yourself. Now go and use it: open Talk and pick 'Die neue Nachbarin'. You will get it wrong, and that is the entire point — the tutor collects your mistakes so the drills can target them.

a1.1-2.title: Zahlen, Zeit, Termine
a1.1-2.intro: Numbers, the clock and arranging a time. This is the unit that gets you through planning a call and paying at a counter.

steps.title: Numbers 13 to 100
steps.body: Thirteen to nineteen are just the digit plus 'zehn'. The tens are the digit plus 'zig'.

items.note: the plural is the same: zwanzig Euro
the cents come after the euros, with no 'and'

steps.title: German says numbers backwards
steps.body: Above twenty, the small digit comes first, joined by 'und'. 21 is 'one-and-twenty'. It feels wrong for about a week and then it stops bothering you.

examples.de: einundzwanzig
zweiunddreißig
siebenundvierzig

steps.note: This is why Germans often repeat phone numbers in pairs, and why you should ask for a number twice.

steps.question: What is 'vierundzwanzig'?
steps.why: vier (4) und zwanzig (20) — the small number is said first, so 24.

steps.title: Telling the time
steps.body: Germans use 'halb' differently from English: halb drei is half *to* three, not half past. It is 2:30.

steps.question: A colleague says the call is 'um halb zehn'. When is it?
steps.why: halb zehn is halfway to ten, so 9:30. This one catches everybody at least once.

items.note: used for anything scheduled, including a doctor or a call
the months sound almost like English
the German word; in tech teams you will also hear das Meeting

steps.title: um, am, von … bis: the little time words
steps.body: English says 'at nine', 'on Monday', 'in May', 'from nine to five'. German has one little word for each, and they do not swap: um for a clock time, am for a day, im for a month, von … bis for a stretch of time. The trap is mixing up um and am, so tie them to a picture: um + Uhr, am + Tag (day).

examples.de: Das Meeting ist um zehn Uhr.
examples.en: The meeting is at ten.

examples.de: Am Montag habe ich einen Termin.
examples.en: On Monday I have an appointment.
examples.note: the day comes first, so the verb comes second

examples.de: Ich arbeite von neun bis fünf.
examples.en: I work from nine to five.

examples.de: Im Mai bin ich in Berlin.
examples.en: In May I am in Berlin.

steps.question: How do you say 'The call is on Tuesday'?
options: Der Anruf ist am Dienstag.
Der Anruf ist um Dienstag.
Der Anruf ist im Dienstag.
steps.why: A day takes am: am Dienstag. um is for a clock time (um zwei Uhr) and im for a month (im Mai).

steps.title: haben — to have
steps.body: After 'sein', this is the verb you will use most. It is irregular too, so again: learn the forms as words.

examples.de: Hast du Zeit?
examples.en: Do you have time?

examples.de: Ich habe einen Termin.
examples.en: I have an appointment.

examples.de: Wir haben ein Meeting um zehn.
examples.en: We have a meeting at ten.

steps.question: Complete it: 'Er ___ einen Termin.'
options: habe
habt
hat
steps.why: er and sie take hat, with no b: ich habe, du hast, er hat. Say 'er hat' a few times; it is short on purpose.

steps.title: Yes/no questions: put the verb first
steps.body: To turn a statement into a question that expects yes or no, move the verb to the front. That is the whole rule — no extra word, no 'do' like in English.

examples.de: Du hast Zeit.
examples.en: You have time.

examples.de: Hast du Zeit?
examples.en: Do you have time?

examples.de: Sprechen Sie Englisch?
examples.en: Do you speak English?

steps.question: How do you ask a colleague 'do you have time on Monday?'
options: Du hast Zeit am Montag?
Hast du Zeit am Montag?
Hast du am Montag Zeit haben?
steps.why: A yes/no question puts the verb first: Hast du …?

steps.title: Regular verbs: one ending per person
steps.body: Most German verbs are regular. Take the stem and add the ending. Once you have this, you have hundreds of verbs.

examples.de: Ich arbeite heute bis fünf.
examples.en: I am working until five today.

examples.de: Wann fangen wir an?
examples.en: When do we start?

examples.de: Er wohnt in Berlin.
examples.en: He lives in Berlin.

examples.de: Wir arbeiten am Freitag zu Hause.
examples.en: We work from home on Friday.

steps.note: arbeiten adds an extra e (du arbeitest, er arbeitet), because 'arbeitst' is almost impossible to say. Most verbs simply take -st and -t: du wohnst, er wohnt.

steps.question: Your colleague Lena works in Berlin. Which is right?
options: Lena arbeiten in Berlin.
Lena arbeite in Berlin.
Lena arbeitet in Berlin.
steps.why: Lena is a 'sie', so the verb ends in -t: sie arbeitet. -e is for ich, -en for wir and Sie.

steps.title: A voicemail from Lena
steps.body: Lena leaves you a voicemail. You will hear it first, then read it. Listen for the day, the time and her phone number. Remember: halb elf is half TO eleven.

lines.de: Hallo {{name}}, hier ist Lena.
lines.en: Hi {{name}}, it's Lena.

lines.de: Hast du am Donnerstag Zeit?
lines.en: Do you have time on Thursday?

lines.de: Wir haben eine Besprechung mit dem Team, von halb elf bis elf.
lines.en: We have a meeting with the team, from half past ten to eleven.

lines.de: Meine Nummer ist null, eins, sieben, zwei, vier, acht, drei, fünf.
lines.en: My number is 0172 4835.

lines.de: Bis Donnerstag, tschüss!
lines.en: See you on Thursday, bye!

lines.de: Hallo {{name}}, hier ist Lena.
lines.en: Hi {{name}}, it's Lena.

lines.de: Hast du am Donnerstag Zeit?
lines.en: Do you have time on Thursday?

lines.de: Die Lerngruppe ist am Donnerstag, von halb elf bis elf.
lines.en: The study group is on Thursday, from half past ten to eleven.

lines.de: Meine Nummer ist null, eins, sieben, zwei, vier, acht, drei, fünf.
lines.en: My number is 0172 4835.

lines.de: Bis Donnerstag, tschüss!
lines.en: See you on Thursday, bye!

steps.question: When does Lena want to meet?
options: Thursday, 11:30 to 12:00
Thursday, 10:30 to 11:00
Tuesday, 10:30 to 11:00
steps.why: 'am Donnerstag, von halb elf bis elf': halb elf is halfway to eleven, so 10:30. Donnerstag is Thursday; Tuesday is Dienstag.

steps.question: What is Lena's phone number?
steps.why: null, eins, sieben, zwei, then vier, acht, drei, fünf. Digits one by one are how Germans give numbers on the phone, and asking 'Noch einmal, bitte' is completely normal.

a1.1-2.outro: Now arrange a time out loud. Open Talk and pick the first scenario — you will need 'um … Uhr' and 'Hast du Zeit?' within the first minute.

a1.1-3.title: Mein Arbeitstag
a1.1-3.intro: Your working day in German: what you do, when you start and how you feel. By the end of this lesson you can give a two-sentence standup update, which is exactly what your team does every morning. Small steps, and every one of them is useful from day one.

student.title: Mein Unitag
student.intro: Your day at university in German: what you study, when you start and how you feel. By the end of this lesson you can tell your study group in two sentences what you are doing today. Small steps, and every one of them is useful from day one.
student.outro: Now say it out loud: open Talk and pick 'In der Lerngruppe'. Lena asks what you are doing today. 'Heute lerne ich …' is a perfect answer, and so is a short one.

steps.title: Words of your working day
steps.body: Many of these are English: German borrowed them. But each one now has der, die or das in front of it. Learn the word together with that little word, always, like a first name and a surname.

items.note: the German word is die Besprechung; tech teams say both

steps.note: The bit after the comma is the plural: das Team, -s means die Teams, and '-' means it does not change (die Server). You do not need plurals yet; they come in the next unit.

student.title: Words of your day at university
student.body: These are the words of a student's day. Each one has der, die or das in front of it. Learn the word together with that little word, always, like a first name and a surname.

items.note: literally 'house work', but it means a written assignment

steps.title: der, die, das: every noun has a gender
steps.body: Every German noun is masculine, feminine or neuter, even a laptop. You see it in 'the': der, die or das. Arabic has genders too, but German ones rarely match and follow no logic: der Laptop, die E-Mail, das Problem. So learn each noun with its der, die or das. 'A' is ein for der and das words, eine for die words. And every German noun starts with a capital letter.

examples.de: Der Server ist neu.
examples.en: The server is new.

examples.de: Das ist ein Problem.
examples.en: That is a problem.

examples.de: Die App ist fertig.
examples.en: The app is ready.

examples.de: Hier ist eine E-Mail.
examples.en: Here is an email.

steps.note: 'Das ist …' (that is) never changes: Das ist der Server, Das ist die App. In that phrase 'das' just means 'that'.

examples.de: Der Kurs ist neu.
examples.en: The course is new.

examples.de: Das ist ein Problem.
examples.en: That is a problem.

examples.de: Die Vorlesung ist um neun.
examples.en: The lecture is at nine.

examples.de: Das ist eine Prüfung.
examples.en: That is an exam.

student.note: 'Das ist …' (that is) never changes: Das ist der Kurs, Das ist die Uni. In that phrase 'das' just means 'that'.

steps.question: It is das Problem. Complete it: 'Das ist ___ Problem.'
options: ein
eine
der
steps.why: das words take ein, just like der words. Only die words take eine: eine E-Mail, eine App. 'der' would be 'the', and Problem is a das word anyway.

steps.title: Your day: verbs and times
steps.body: The verbs of a normal day, and the parts of the day. Some verbs here have a little front part (an, auf): the next page shows what happens to it.

steps.title: Verbs that split: ich fange um neun an
steps.body: Some German verbs come in two parts: an + fangen = anfangen (to start). In a sentence, the main part takes the normal verb slot, second, and the little front part jumps to the very end. English does something similar with 'I get up'. The trap is forgetting the little part: 'Ich fange um neun' sounds unfinished to a German ear, like a sentence holding its breath.

examples.de: Ich stehe um halb sieben auf.
examples.en: I get up at half past six.

examples.de: Wann fängst du an?
examples.en: When do you start?
examples.note: in a question too, the little part goes to the end

examples.de: Wir hören um fünf auf.
examples.en: We stop at five.

examples.de: Jonas ruft heute an.
examples.en: Jonas is calling today.

steps.note: How to spot these verbs: in the dictionary they start with a little word like an- or auf-. Say the sentence and finish it with that little word.

steps.question: Which one is right?
options: Ich fange um neun.
Ich anfange um neun.
Ich fange um neun an.
steps.why: fangen sits in second place and 'an' goes to the very end. Without the 'an' the sentence is not finished, and 'ich anfange' is not how German says it in a main sentence.

steps.title: Time first, verb still second
steps.body: You know the rule: the verb is second. Germans love to start a sentence with the time: Um neun Uhr …, Heute …, Am Abend … The verb then comes right after the time, and ich moves behind the verb. Arabic and English both want 'Um neun Uhr ich fange an'. Think of it as three beats: time, verb, me.

examples.de: Um neun Uhr fange ich an.
examples.en: At nine I start.

examples.de: Am Morgen bin ich müde.
examples.en: In the morning I'm tired.

examples.de: Um zwölf Uhr esse ich.
examples.en: At twelve I eat.

examples.de: Dann mache ich Pause.
examples.en: Then I take a break.

steps.note: This takes weeks to become automatic, for everybody. Each time the tutor corrects it, your ear gets a little better.

steps.question: You start with the time. Which one is right?
options: Um sieben Uhr stehe ich auf.
Um sieben Uhr ich stehe auf.
Um sieben Uhr ich aufstehe.
steps.why: Time first, then the verb (stehe), then ich, and 'auf' at the very end. Both wrong options put ich before the verb.

steps.title: Everyone else: wir, ihr, sie
steps.body: In unit 2 you learned ich arbeite and du arbeitest. Here are the rest, and there is good news: wir, sie (they) and Sie (polite 'you') always look exactly like the dictionary form of the verb. Only ihr is new. English has one 'you'; German has three: du for one friend, ihr for two or more friends, Sie for anyone formal, one person or many.

examples.de: Wir machen um zwölf Pause.
examples.en: We take a break at twelve.

examples.de: Was macht ihr heute?
examples.en: What are you doing today?

examples.de: Lena und Jonas wohnen in Berlin.
examples.en: Lena and Jonas live in Berlin.

examples.de: Wir lernen Deutsch.
examples.en: We are learning German.

steps.note: es (it) works like er and sie. You already know it from 'Es ist drei Uhr'.

steps.question: You ask two friends: 'What are you doing today?'
options: Was machst du heute?
Was macht ihr heute?
Was machen ihr heute?
steps.why: Two friends are ihr, and ihr takes -t: ihr macht. 'Was machst du?' would ask only one of them.

steps.title: Ich arbeite als … bei …: saying what you do
steps.body: To say what you do, use als (as) for the job and bei (at, for) for the company. And one surprise: no 'a' before a job. English says 'I am an engineer'; German says 'Ich bin Ingenieur', with no ein. A woman adds -in: Ingenieurin, Entwicklerin.

head: German
English
rows: Ich arbeite bei einer Firma in Berlin.
I work for a company in Berlin.
What do you do for a living?

examples.de: Ich bin {{role_de}}.
examples.en: I am a DevOps engineer.

examples.de: Ich arbeite als {{role_de}}.
examples.en: I work as a DevOps engineer.

examples.de: Ich arbeite bei einer Firma in Berlin.
examples.en: I work for a company in Berlin.
examples.note: learn 'bei einer Firma' as one block

examples.de: Was bist du von Beruf?
examples.en: What do you do for a living?

student.title: Ich studiere … an der …: saying what you study
student.body: To say what you study, use studieren with the subject, and no 'the': Ich studiere Maschinenbau. The place comes with an der: an der Universität, an der Uni. And one surprise: no 'a' before what you are. English says 'I am a student'; German says 'Ich bin Studentin', with no eine. A woman adds -in: Student, Studentin.

head: German
English
rows: I am a mechanical engineering student.
Ich studiere an der Uni in Amman.
I study at the university in Amman.

examples.de: Ich studiere Maschinenbau.
examples.en: I study mechanical engineering.

examples.de: Ich studiere an der Uni in Amman.
examples.en: I study at the university in Amman.
examples.note: learn 'an der Uni' as one block

examples.de: Ich bin Studentin.
examples.en: I am a student.
examples.note: no eine; a man says 'Ich bin Student'

examples.de: Was studierst du?
examples.en: What do you study?

steps.question: How do you say 'I am a developer'?
options: Ich bin ein Entwickler.
Ich arbeite bei Entwickler.
Ich bin Entwickler.
steps.why: Germans say a job with no ein: Ich bin Entwickler. bei is for the company: Ich arbeite bei einer Firma.

student.question: How do you say 'I study mechanical engineering'?
options: Ich studiere an Maschinenbau.
Ich studiere den Maschinenbau.
Ich studiere Maschinenbau.
student.why: The subject comes straight after studieren, with no 'the'. an der is for the place: an der Uni.

steps.title: How you are
steps.body: Short answers you will use every day: in a standup, on a call, with a neighbour. After 'ich bin', a word like müde never changes, for a man or a woman.

items.note: informal; to Sie: Wie geht es Ihnen?
said with a sigh, it also means 'I'm exhausted'

steps.title: The morning standup
steps.body: Lena runs the daily standup: everyone says in a sentence or two what they are doing today. You will hear it first, then read it. Listen for what Jonas does in the afternoon, and what Mira needs.

lines.de: Guten Morgen! Jonas, was machst du heute?
lines.en: Good morning! Jonas, what are you doing today?

lines.de: Heute teste ich die App. Am Nachmittag habe ich ein Meeting.
lines.en: Today I'm testing the app. In the afternoon I have a meeting.

lines.de: Danke. Und du, Mira?
lines.en: Thanks. And you, Mira?

lines.de: Ich schreibe Code. Aber ich habe ein Problem.
lines.en: I'm writing code. But I have a problem.

lines.de: Okay. Wir sprechen um elf Uhr.
lines.en: Okay. We'll talk at eleven.

lines.de: Super, danke!
lines.en: Great, thanks!

student.title: The study group
student.body: Lena opens the study group: everyone says in a sentence or two what they are doing today. You will hear it first, then read it. Listen for what Jonas does in the afternoon, and what Mira needs.

lines.de: Hallo! Jonas, was machst du heute?
lines.en: Hi! Jonas, what are you doing today?

lines.de: Heute lerne ich Mathe. Am Nachmittag habe ich eine Vorlesung.
lines.en: Today I'm studying maths. In the afternoon I have a lecture.

lines.de: Danke. Und du, Mira?
lines.en: Thanks. And you, Mira?

lines.de: Ich schreibe die Hausarbeit. Aber ich habe ein Problem.
lines.en: I'm writing the term paper. But I have a problem.

lines.de: Okay. Wir sprechen um elf Uhr.
lines.en: Okay. We'll talk at eleven.

lines.de: Super, danke!
lines.en: Great, thanks!

steps.question: What does Jonas do in the afternoon?
options: He tests the app.
He has a meeting.
He writes code.
steps.why: 'Am Nachmittag habe ich ein Meeting.' Testing the app is what he does first, today. Notice the order: time first (am Nachmittag), then the verb.

options: He studies maths.
He has a lecture.
He writes a term paper.
student.why: 'Am Nachmittag habe ich eine Vorlesung.' Maths is what he studies first, today. Notice the order: time first (am Nachmittag), then the verb.

steps.question: What about Mira?
options: She has a problem, and Lena will talk with her at eleven.
She is tired and stops at eleven.
Everything is fine: she has no problem.
steps.why: 'Aber ich habe ein Problem.' and Lena answers 'Wir sprechen um elf Uhr.' In a real standup, 'Ich habe ein Problem' is all you need to say: the details come after.

a1.1-3.outro: Now give your own update: open Talk and pick 'Das Daily Standup'. Lena asks what you are doing today. 'Heute teste ich die App' is a perfect answer, and so is a short one.

a1.1-4.title: Essen und Einkaufen
a1.1-4.intro: Food, shopping and paying. By the end of this lesson you can order at a bakery or a café, find things in a supermarket, say what you do not eat, and pay and tip like a local. You will use this the very first day you are in Germany.

steps.title: At the bakery
steps.body: German bakeries are everywhere, and they open early. These words get you through the counter. Bread rolls (Brötchen) are the German breakfast.

items.note: in the south of Germany: die Semmel
what you hear behind the counter, often 'Was darf's sein?'

steps.title: Ich möchte … and Ich hätte gern …: asking politely
steps.body: Two fixed phrases get you through every counter in Germany. 'Ich möchte …' means 'I would like …'. 'Ich hätte gern …' means the same and is what you hear most at a counter. Do not worry about the grammar inside them: learn them as blocks, then add what you want and 'bitte'. Be careful with 'Ich will …': it means 'I want …' and sounds pushy at a counter.

examples.de: Ich möchte ein Brötchen, bitte.
examples.en: I'd like a bread roll, please.

examples.de: Ich hätte gern eine Brezel.
examples.en: I'd like a pretzel.

examples.de: Möchten Sie noch etwas?
examples.en: Would you like anything else?
examples.note: you will hear this a lot; answer 'Nein, danke. Das ist alles.'

examples.de: Was möchtest du trinken?
examples.en: What would you like to drink?
examples.note: the second verb (trinken) goes to the end

steps.question: At the bakery, which is the polite way to ask for a bread roll?
options: Ich will ein Brötchen.
Ich hätte gern ein Brötchen.
Ich habe gern ein Brötchen.
steps.why: 'Ich hätte gern …' is the counter phrase. 'Ich will' means 'I want' and sounds pushy. 'Ich habe gern' means 'I like having', which is not a request at all.

steps.title: der becomes den when you order it
steps.body: When a noun is the thing you take, want, have or order, German changes der to den and ein to einen. This is called the accusative. The good news: only der words change. die and das words stay exactly as they are. English does this only with he and him; German does it with 'the' and 'a' too. 'Ich nehme …' (literally 'I take') is how Germans say 'I'll have …'.

examples.de: Ich nehme den Kuchen.
examples.en: I'll have the cake.

examples.de: Ich möchte einen Tee, bitte.
examples.en: I'd like a tea, please.

examples.de: Ich hätte gern einen Kaffee.
examples.en: I'd like a coffee.

examples.de: Wir nehmen die Pizza und das Wasser.
examples.en: We'll have the pizza and the water.

steps.note: Only one thing to remember for now: der word + order = den or einen.

steps.question: You order a coffee (der Kaffee). Which is right?
options: Ich nehme ein Kaffee.
Ich nehme der Kaffee.
Ich nehme einen Kaffee.
steps.why: Kaffee is a der word, and it is the thing you order, so ein becomes einen. With a die or das word nothing would change: eine Pizza, ein Wasser.

steps.title: In the supermarket
steps.body: The sections of a supermarket, and how you ask for an amount. German says 'a bottle water', with no word for 'of'.
steps.note: Halal meat is easiest to find at Turkish and Arabic shops and butchers; in a supermarket, look for 'halal' on the packet.

steps.title: More than one: plurals
steps.body: English adds -s. German has a few patterns, and the honest answer is: learn the plural with the word, the way you learn der, die, das. Two pieces of good news. First, in the plural 'the' is always die, whatever the gender. Second, the patterns below cover most food words.

examples.de: Ich hätte gern zwei Brötchen.
examples.en: I'd like two bread rolls.

examples.de: Ich nehme drei Brezeln.
examples.en: I'll take three pretzels.

examples.de: Die Äpfel sind da hinten.
examples.en: The apples are back there.

examples.de: Wir brauchen sechs Eier.
examples.en: We need six eggs.

steps.note: There is no 'ein' in the plural: ein Apfel, but just Äpfel.

steps.question: You want two eggs (das Ei). What do you say?
options: Zwei Eier, bitte.
Zwei Eis, bitte.
Zwei Ei, bitte.
steps.why: das Ei, die Eier: the + er pattern. 'Eis' is ice cream, which is a very different order.

steps.title: kein and nicht: saying no
steps.body: German has two words for 'not'. Use kein before a noun that would have ein, or no word at all: it means 'no' or 'not a'. Use nicht for everything else, for example with an adjective like teuer (expensive) or heiß (hot). kein takes the same endings as ein, so in an order it is keinen for der words. And notice: 'I don't eat pork' is simply 'Ich esse kein Schweinefleisch'. No 'don't', just kein.

examples.de: Ich esse kein Schweinefleisch.
examples.en: I don't eat pork.

examples.de: Ich trinke keinen Alkohol.
examples.en: I don't drink alcohol.

examples.de: Der Kaffee ist nicht heiß.
examples.en: The coffee isn't hot.

examples.de: Das ist nicht teuer.
examples.en: That isn't expensive.

steps.note: A quick test: if English could say 'a …' or nothing before the noun (a coffee, meat), German uses kein. Otherwise, nicht.

steps.question: How do you say 'I don't eat meat'?
options: Ich esse nicht Fleisch.
Ich nicht esse Fleisch.
Ich esse kein Fleisch.
steps.why: Fleisch is a noun with no ein in front, so 'not' becomes kein: Ich esse kein Fleisch. And the verb stays in second place.

steps.title: ja, nein and doch
steps.body: To a normal question, answer ja (yes) or nein (no). But when the question already has a 'not' in it, like 'Don't you want a coffee?', German has a third word: doch. Doch means 'yes, I do!', against the 'not'. In English, 'yes' to a question like that is unclear. In German, doch is perfectly clear, and Germans use it all the time.

examples.de: Doch, ich möchte einen Kaffee.
examples.en: Yes, I do want a coffee.

examples.de: Nein, ich esse kein Fleisch.
examples.en: No, I don't eat meat.

examples.de: Doch, ich habe Hunger.
examples.en: Yes, I am hungry.
examples.note: after 'Hast du keinen Hunger?' Literally: I have hunger

examples.de: Ja, ich nehme den Tee.
examples.en: Yes, I'll have the tea.
examples.note: after a normal question: 'Nehmen Sie den Tee?'

steps.note: Answering 'ja' to a 'not' question confuses people. If you mean yes, say doch.

steps.question: A colleague asks: 'Trinkst du keinen Tee?' You DO drink tea. What do you say?
options: Doch, ich trinke Tee.
Ja, ich trinke keinen Tee.
Nein, ich trinke Tee.
steps.why: The question has a 'not' in it (keinen), and your answer goes against it: yes, I do. That is exactly what doch is for. 'Nein' would mean you do not drink tea.

steps.title: In a café or restaurant
steps.body: Ordering, asking what is in a dish, and paying. In Germany you usually pay at the table, and the waiter often asks if you pay together or separately.

items.note: das Menü is a set meal, not the menu
what the waiter asks when you pay
how Germans tip: round up by about 5 to 10 percent and say this

steps.title: In the café
steps.body: A guest orders in a café. You will hear it first, then read it. Listen for two things: does the guest want cake, and how much do they pay in the end?

lines.de: Guten Tag! Was möchten Sie trinken?
lines.en: Hello! What would you like to drink?

lines.de: Ich hätte gern einen Tee, bitte.
lines.en: I'd like a tea, please.

lines.de: Nur einen Tee? Keinen Kuchen?
lines.en: Just a tea? No cake?

lines.de: Doch! Ein Stück Apfelkuchen, bitte.
lines.en: Oh yes! A piece of apple cake, please.

lines.de: Gern. Das macht sechs Euro fünfzig.
lines.en: Sure. That comes to six euros fifty.

lines.de: Hier sind sieben Euro. Stimmt so.
lines.en: Here's seven euros. Keep the change.

steps.question: What does the guest order?
options: A tea and a piece of apple cake
Just a tea, no cake
A coffee and a piece of cake
steps.why: 'Keinen Kuchen?' — 'Doch!' Doch goes against the 'not': yes, I do want cake. Then the guest orders 'ein Stück Apfelkuchen'.

steps.question: How much does the guest pay in the end?
steps.why: The bill is sechs Euro fünfzig (€6.50). The guest gives sieben Euro and says 'Stimmt so': the 50 cents are the tip.

a1.1-4.outro: Now go shopping for real: open Talk and pick 'In der Bäckerei'. 'Ich hätte gern zwei Brötchen' is all you need to start, and the woman behind the counter will help with the rest.

a1.1-5.title: Wo ist …?
a1.1-5.intro: Finding your way. By the end of this lesson you can ask where something is, understand simple directions, and ask people to repeat or slow down. That last part matters most: with it, you can never really get lost.

steps.title: Places in the city and in a building
steps.body: The places you will look for in your first weeks, and the parts of a building. 'Wo ist …?' plus one of these is already a complete question.

items.note: the ground floor is das Erdgeschoss; the first floor is one floor up

steps.title: es gibt: there is, there are
steps.body: To ask if something is nearby, Germans say 'Gibt es hier …?' (Is there … here?). es gibt is a fixed block: it means both 'there is' and 'there are'. What comes after it works like ordering food in the last unit: der becomes den and ein becomes einen; die and das stay the same. kein works too: Es gibt keinen Bus.

examples.de: Gibt es hier einen Supermarkt?
examples.en: Is there a supermarket here?

examples.de: Es gibt eine Apotheke am Bahnhof.
examples.en: There's a pharmacy at the station.

examples.de: Hier gibt es keinen Bus.
examples.en: There's no bus here.
examples.note: hier first, so the verb gibt comes second

examples.de: Ja, es gibt einen Aufzug.
examples.en: Yes, there's a lift.

steps.question: You need a pharmacy (die Apotheke). Which is right?
options: Gibt es hier eine Apotheke?
Gibt es hier einen Apotheke?
Es gibt hier Apotheke?
steps.why: Apotheke is a die word, and die words do not change: eine Apotheke. einen is only for der words, like einen Supermarkt.

steps.title: Directions: learn them as blocks
steps.body: Directions are where German grammar gets in the way, so do not build them: learn them whole. These blocks cover almost every answer you will hear. Listen for the key word first: links, rechts or geradeaus already tells you most of the way.

head: German
English
rows: the first street on the left
the second street on the right

examples.de: Die Apotheke ist links.
examples.en: The pharmacy is on the left.

examples.de: Der Supermarkt ist gegenüber.
examples.en: The supermarket is opposite.

examples.de: Die Bank ist neben der Post.
examples.en: The bank is next to the post office.

examples.de: Die Haltestelle ist da vorne.
examples.en: The stop is up there.

steps.note: erste = first, zweite = second, dritte = third. Almost nobody gives more than three steps.

steps.question: Someone says 'die zweite Straße links'. Where do you go?
options: The second street on the right
The second street on the left
Straight on, then the first left
steps.why: zweite = second, links = left. rechts would be right, and erste would be first.

steps.title: Getting around
steps.body: German cities run on buses, trams and trains. These are the words on the signs and in the announcements.

items.note: in most cities you buy it before you get on

steps.title: Gehen Sie …! Instructions, the polite way
steps.body: When someone gives you directions, they use the Sie form with the verb first: 'Gehen Sie geradeaus.' It looks like a yes/no question, but the voice goes down at the end, not up. This is polite German, not bossy, especially with bitte. With a verb that splits, the little part still goes to the end: Steigen Sie hier aus (get off here).

examples.de: Gehen Sie hier links.
examples.en: Go left here.

examples.de: Nehmen Sie die U-Bahn.
examples.en: Take the underground.

examples.de: Gehen Sie die erste Straße rechts.
examples.en: Take the first street on the right.

examples.de: Steigen Sie am Hauptbahnhof aus.
examples.en: Get off at the main station.

steps.note: You mostly need to understand this one, not say it. Hear the verb first and a full stop: it is an instruction.

steps.question: Someone says 'Nehmen Sie den Bus.' What do they mean?
options: Are you taking the bus?
Take the bus.
They are taking the bus.
steps.why: Verb first, Sie, and the voice going down: an instruction. As a question it would sound different, with the voice going up: 'Nehmen Sie den Bus?'

steps.title: When you do not understand
steps.body: Some of these you know from unit 1. Directions come fast, so these are the most useful words in this lesson. Use them as often as you need: Germans are used to it and happy to repeat.

items.en: Excuse me, can you help me?

steps.title: Können Sie …? Asking for help politely
steps.body: 'Können Sie …?' means 'Can you …?', and it is the polite way to ask for almost anything. können comes first in the question, and the action goes to the very end in its dictionary form: Können Sie das wiederholen? So the sentence opens with one verb and closes with the other, like the verbs that split. Add bitte and you are as polite as anyone needs to be.

examples.de: Können Sie mir helfen?
examples.en: Can you help me?
examples.note: mir = me; learn it as a block

examples.de: Können Sie das bitte wiederholen?
examples.en: Can you repeat that, please?

examples.de: Können Sie langsamer sprechen?
examples.en: Can you speak more slowly?

examples.de: Ich kann das nicht lesen.
examples.en: I can't read that.

steps.note: ich kann and er kann have no ending at all. That is normal for this kind of verb, and you will meet more of them soon.

steps.question: You did not understand. How do you ask 'Can you repeat that?'
options: Können Sie wiederholen das?
Kann Sie das wiederholen?
Können Sie das wiederholen?
steps.why: Sie goes with können, and the action (wiederholen) goes to the very end. 'kann' is for ich and er, not for Sie.

steps.title: Is there a pharmacy here?
steps.body: You ask a woman in the street for a pharmacy. You will hear it first, then read it. Listen for the way, and for how far it is.

lines.de: Entschuldigung, können Sie mir helfen? Gibt es hier eine Apotheke?
lines.en: Excuse me, can you help me? Is there a pharmacy here?

lines.de: Ja. Gehen Sie hier geradeaus und dann die zweite Straße links.
lines.en: Yes. Go straight on here and then the second street on the left.

lines.de: Wie bitte? Langsamer, bitte.
lines.en: Sorry? Slower, please.

lines.de: Geradeaus, dann die zweite Straße links. Die Apotheke ist neben der Bank.
lines.en: Straight on, then the second street on the left. The pharmacy is next to the bank.

lines.de: Ist das weit?
lines.en: Is it far?

lines.de: Nein, nur fünf Minuten zu Fuß.
lines.en: No, only five minutes on foot.

steps.question: Where is the pharmacy?
options: Straight on, then the second street on the left, next to the bank
The first street on the right, opposite the bank
Straight on, then the second street on the right, next to the post office
steps.why: 'Geradeaus, dann die zweite Straße links. Die Apotheke ist neben der Bank.' And notice what made it easy: 'Langsamer, bitte' got the whole thing said again, slowly.

steps.question: How far is it?
options: Fifteen minutes by bus
Five minutes on foot
Far: take the U-Bahn
steps.why: 'nur fünf Minuten zu Fuß': only five minutes on foot. fünf is 5; fünfzehn would be 15.

a1.1-5.outro: That is the whole of A1.1: well done. Now try it out loud: open Talk and pick 'Wo ist die Ausländerbehörde?'. Ask the way, and ask for 'Noch einmal, bitte' at least once, even if you understood.

a1.2-1.title: Im Team
a1.2-1.intro: Working with other people in German: asking for help, saying what you can, must and want to do, and saying when you do not understand. After this lesson you can ask a colleague for a review and tell them by when you need it.

student.title: In der Lerngruppe
student.intro: Working with other people in German: asking for help, saying what you can, must and want to do, and saying when you do not understand. After this lesson you can ask a fellow student to read your lab report and tell them by when you need it.
student.outro: Now ask for help out loud: open Talk and pick 'Kannst du meinen Laborbericht lesen?'. Say what the report is about in one sentence, and give a time with 'bis'.

steps.title: The developer's day
steps.body: Tech German borrows English words and gives them a German article. Learn the article with the word: it decides every ending you will meet in this lesson.

items.note: bis + a time = by / until that time

student.title: The student's day
student.body: Learn every noun with its article: it decides every ending you will meet in this lesson.

items.note: bis + a time = by / until that time

steps.title: können, müssen, wollen: the sentence bracket
steps.body: können (can), müssen (must, have to) and wollen (want to) take a second verb, like English 'can'. German sends that second verb to the very end, unchanged. The modal sits in position two, the infinitive closes the sentence, and everything else goes in between, like a bracket. The trap is English order: not 'Ich muss arbeiten heute' but 'Ich muss heute arbeiten'. ich and er share one form: ich kann, er kann.

examples.de: Ich muss heute den Server neu starten.
examples.en: I have to restart the server today.

examples.de: Kannst du mir helfen?
examples.en: Can you help me?

examples.de: Ich will das Ticket heute fertig machen.
examples.en: I want to finish the ticket today.

examples.de: Ich kann das nicht allein machen.
examples.en: I can't do that on my own.

steps.note: 'Ich will' means 'I want to', not 'I will'. It is one of the classic false friends for English speakers.

examples.de: Ich muss heute den Bericht abgeben.
examples.en: I have to hand in the report today.
examples.note: a separable verb stays in one piece at the end

examples.de: Kannst du mir helfen?
examples.en: Can you help me?

examples.de: Ich will die Aufgabe heute fertig machen.
examples.en: I want to finish the assignment today.

examples.de: Ich kann das nicht allein machen.
examples.en: I can't do that on my own.

steps.question: How do you say 'I have to work today'?
options: Ich muss arbeiten heute.
Ich muss heute arbeiten.
Ich muss heute arbeite.
steps.why: muss takes position two and the infinitive arbeiten goes to the very end. After a modal verb the second verb never takes an ending: arbeiten, not arbeite.

steps.title: The du imperative: asking a colleague
steps.body: To ask someone you say du to, take the du form and drop du and the -st: du schaust → Schau!, du wartest → Warte! On its own it can sound like an order, so add bitte or mal (mal softens it, like 'just'). Verbs that change e to i keep the i: du hilfst → Hilf mir! A separable verb sends its prefix to the end: Ruf mich an!

examples.de: Schau mal, hier ist der Fehler.
examples.en: Look, here is the error.

examples.de: Schick mir bitte den Link.
examples.en: Please send me the link.

examples.de: Warte kurz, ich komme gleich.
examples.en: Wait a moment, I'm coming.

examples.de: Ruf mich morgen an.
examples.en: Call me tomorrow.

steps.note: With Sie it works differently: the Sie form with Sie after it, as you learned in A1.1: Warten Sie bitte.

steps.question: You want a colleague to send you the file. What do you write in the chat?
options: Schickst mir bitte die Datei.
Schicken mir bitte die Datei.
Schick mir bitte die Datei.
steps.why: du schickst → drop du, drop -st → Schick. 'Schickst mir' is a question with the du missing, and 'Schicken' needs Sie after it: Schicken Sie mir bitte …

steps.title: Asking for and offering help
steps.body: Short, friendly, and you can use them every day. In German teams it is completely normal to ask; nobody expects you to struggle alone.

items.en: By when do you need it?

steps.note: helfen takes mir and dir, not mich and dich. That is the dative, which comes in A2.1; for now, learn 'Kannst du mir helfen?' as one block.

steps.title: mein, dein, sein, ihr: whose is it?
steps.body: These are my, your, his, her, our, your (formal). They take the endings of ein / eine: mein Laptop, meine Aufgabe, and in the accusative a der-word gets -en: Ich suche meinen Laptop. Arabic adds 'my' to the end of the noun; German puts a word in front, and its ending follows the noun's gender, not the owner's. The trap: sein = his, ihr = her, and Ihr with a capital = your (Sie).

examples.de: Ist dein Laptop neu?
examples.en: Is your laptop new?

examples.de: Mira sucht ihren Schlüssel.
examples.en: Mira is looking for her key.

examples.de: Unsere Wohnung ist klein.
examples.en: Our flat is small.

examples.de: Wie ist Ihre E-Mail-Adresse?
examples.en: What is your email address?

examples.de: Ich finde meinen Fehler nicht.
examples.en: I can't find my mistake.

steps.question: Jonas cannot find his phone (das Handy). Which sentence is right?
options: Jonas sucht sein Handy.
Jonas sucht ihr Handy.
Jonas sucht seinen Handy.
steps.why: Jonas is a man, so 'his' is sein; ihr would be her. das Handy is neuter, and das-words take no ending in the accusative: sein Handy. seinen is only for der-words.

steps.title: brauchen, haben, suchen, finden + accusative
steps.body: These four verbs always have a direct object, and that object is in the accusative. You know the rule from A1.1: only der-words change (der → den, ein → einen, kein → keinen). die and das stay as they are. So: Ich brauche einen Laptop, but Ich brauche eine Pause and ein Passwort. Every time you use one of these verbs, ask yourself: is the thing a der-word?

examples.de: Ich brauche das Passwort.
examples.en: I need the password.

examples.de: Hast du einen Moment?
examples.en: Do you have a moment?

examples.de: Ich suche den Fehler.
examples.en: I'm looking for the error.

examples.de: Wir haben keinen Drucker.
examples.en: We don't have a printer.

steps.note: finden also means 'to think, to find': Ich finde das gut = I think that's good.

steps.question: der Laptop is a der-word. Which sentence is correct?
options: Ich brauche ein Laptop.
Ich brauche einen Laptop.
Ich brauche einer Laptop.
steps.why: brauchen takes the accusative, and in the accusative a der-word's ein becomes einen. With die Datei or das Passwort nothing would change: eine Datei, ein Passwort.

steps.title: mich, dich, ihn: people as the object
steps.body: When a person is the object (call me, I understand you), German uses a second set of pronouns. Only three look new: mich, dich and ihn. The rest are the same as the subject forms. ihn is also 'it' for any der-word: Der Link? Ich schicke ihn. A pronoun for a thing follows the noun's gender, so a laptop is 'he' in German, and that is perfectly normal.

examples.de: Kannst du mich anrufen?
examples.en: Can you call me?

examples.de: Ich verstehe dich nicht.
examples.en: I don't understand you.

examples.de: Der Link? Ich schicke ihn gleich.
examples.en: The link? I'll send it in a moment.

examples.de: Frau Sommer sucht Sie.
examples.en: Ms Sommer is looking for you.

examples.de: Wir brauchen euch morgen.
examples.en: We need you (all) tomorrow.

steps.note: helfen is the exception you met above: Kannst du mir helfen?, never mich. You will see why in A2.1.

steps.question: A colleague says: 'Ich rufe dich morgen an.' What does it mean?
options: Call me tomorrow.
I'll call you tomorrow.
You'll call me tomorrow.
steps.why: ich is the one who calls, dich (you) is the one who gets called. 'Call me' would be 'Ruf mich an'. And the present tense often means the future in German: Ich rufe … an = I'll call.

steps.title: When you don't understand
steps.body: At work you will not understand everything, and saying so is a skill, not a weakness. These phrases get you an explanation instead of a nod.

items.de: Wie sagt man das auf Deutsch?
items.en: How do you say that in German?
Can you write that down, please?

steps.title: A message in the team chat
steps.body: Your colleague Jonas writes to you in the team chat. Read it and look for three things: what his problem is, what he needs from you, and when you can help.

lines.de: Hallo {{name}}, hast du kurz Zeit? Mein Test funktioniert nicht, und ich finde den Fehler nicht.
lines.en: Hi {{name}}, do you have a minute? My test doesn't work, and I can't find the bug.

lines.de: Kannst du bitte meinen Pull Request anschauen? Ich muss die Änderung heute fertig machen.
lines.en: Can you please look at my pull request? I have to finish the change today.

lines.de: Klar, ich helfe dir gern. Aber ich habe jetzt ein Meeting. Ist um drei okay?
lines.en: Sure, I'm happy to help. But I have a meeting now. Is three okay?

lines.de: Um drei ist super. Ich schicke dir den Link. Danke!
lines.en: Three is great. I'll send you the link. Thanks!

lines.de: Kein Problem. Bis später!
lines.en: No problem. See you later!

student.title: A message from a fellow student
student.body: Jonas, who is in your lab course, writes to you. Read it and look for three things: what his problem is, what he needs from you, and when you can help.

lines.de: Hallo {{name}}, hast du kurz Zeit? Mein Ergebnis stimmt nicht, und ich finde den Fehler nicht.
lines.en: Hi {{name}}, do you have a minute? My result is wrong, and I can't find the mistake.

lines.de: Kannst du bitte meinen Laborbericht lesen? Ich muss ihn heute abgeben.
lines.en: Can you please read my lab report? I have to hand it in today.

lines.de: Klar, ich helfe dir gern. Aber ich habe jetzt eine Vorlesung. Ist um drei okay?
lines.en: Sure, I'm happy to help. But I have a lecture now. Is three okay?

lines.de: Um drei ist super. Ich schicke dir die Datei. Danke!
lines.en: Three is great. I'll send you the file. Thanks!

lines.de: Kein Problem. Bis später!
lines.en: No problem. See you later!

steps.question: What does Jonas want from you?
options: He wants to join your meeting.
He wants you to look at his pull request.
He wants you to write his test.
steps.why: 'Kannst du bitte meinen Pull Request anschauen?' — anschauen means to look at. The meeting is yours, and it is the reason you can only help at three.

options: He wants to come to your lecture.
He wants you to read his lab report.
He wants you to write his report.
student.why: 'Kannst du bitte meinen Laborbericht lesen?' — he wants you to read it, not write it. The lecture is yours, and it is the reason you can only help at three.

steps.question: When will you help him?
options: Right now
Tomorrow
At three
steps.why: 'Ist um drei okay?' — 'Um drei ist super.' He needs it today, but you are busy until three.

a1.2-1.outro: Now ask for help out loud: open Talk and pick 'Bitte um ein Code-Review'. Say what the change does in one sentence, and give a time with 'bis'.

a1.2-2.title: Freizeit und Wochenende
a1.2-2.intro: Free time, sport, the weather and your home city. After this lesson you can say what you like doing and how often, make small talk about the weather, and tell a German something about Amman.

steps.title: Hobbies and sport
steps.body: Most hobbies are just a verb, sometimes with a noun in front: Fußball spielen, Musik hören. In a sentence the verb moves to position two and the noun stays: Ich spiele Fußball.
steps.note: Germany runs on clubs: if you want to play football or volleyball there, you join a Verein.

steps.title: Verbs that change their vowel
steps.body: A few very common verbs change their vowel, but only with du and er / sie / es; ich, wir and Sie stay normal. a becomes ä (du fährst), e becomes i or ie (du isst, du liest, du siehst). Two persons, one change: that is the whole rule. 'Er fahrt' or 'du lest' will be understood, but they sound wrong to every German.

examples.de: Fährst du oft Rad?
examples.en: Do you cycle often?

examples.de: Am Sonntag schläft er lange.
examples.en: On Sunday he sleeps in.

examples.de: Was liest du gerade?
examples.en: What are you reading at the moment?

examples.de: Sie isst kein Fleisch.
examples.en: She doesn't eat meat.

steps.note: du isst and du liest: the s of the stem and the -st ending merge, so there is only one s sound.

steps.question: Jonas likes cycling. Which sentence is right?
options: Jonas fahrt gern Rad.
Jonas fährt gern Rad.
Jonas fahre gern Rad.
steps.why: fahren changes a to ä with du and er / sie: er fährt. fahre is the ich form.

steps.title: gern, lieber, am liebsten
steps.body: German has no verb for 'to like doing'. You take the normal verb and add gern: Ich schwimme gern = I like swimming. For what you prefer, use lieber; for your favourite, am liebsten. gern sits right after the verb (or after the object): Ich spiele gern Fußball. For things rather than activities, use mögen: Ich mag Kaffee. 'Ich mag schwimmen' is understood, but it sounds translated.

head: German
English
rows: Am liebsten lese ich am Abend.
I like reading in the evening best.

examples.de: Ich spiele gern Fußball.
examples.en: I like playing football.

examples.de: Schwimmst du gern?
examples.en: Do you like swimming?

examples.de: Ich trinke lieber Tee.
examples.en: I prefer tea.

examples.de: Am liebsten gehe ich ins Kino.
examples.en: Most of all I like going to the cinema.

steps.note: Am liebsten at the start takes position one, so the verb comes next: Am liebsten gehe ich …, never 'Am liebsten ich gehe'.

steps.question: How do you say 'I like cooking'?
options: Ich mag kochen.
Ich gern koche.
Ich koche gern.
steps.why: The verb stays in position two and gern follows it: Ich koche gern. 'Ich mag kochen' is understood, but for activities Germans say gern.

steps.title: When and how often: am, im, um, oft, nie
steps.body: Three small words for 'on, in, at'. am for days and parts of the day (am Montag, am Wochenende, am Abend), im for months and seasons (im Juli, im Sommer), um for clock times (um acht Uhr). How often: immer, oft, manchmal, selten, nie, and jeden Tag, jede Woche. They usually go right after the verb. If you start the sentence with one of them, the verb still comes second: Am Samstag spiele ich Fußball.

head: word
for
example
rows: days, the weekend, parts of the day
am Freitag, am Wochenende, am Abend

examples.de: Am Wochenende schlafe ich lange.
examples.en: At the weekend I sleep in.

examples.de: Im Sommer ist es in Amman heiß.
examples.en: In summer it is hot in Amman.

examples.de: Ich gehe jeden Tag ins Fitnessstudio.
examples.en: I go to the gym every day.

examples.de: Am Abend spielen wir manchmal Fußball.
examples.en: In the evening we sometimes play football.

examples.de: Ich esse nie Fleisch.
examples.en: I never eat meat.

steps.note: One exception you will hear a lot: in der Nacht (at night), not 'am Nacht'.

steps.question: 'We play football on Saturday.' Which one is right?
options: Wir spielen am Samstag Fußball.
Wir spielen im Samstag Fußball.
Wir spielen um Samstag Fußball.
steps.why: Days take am. im is for months and seasons (im Mai), um for clock times (um acht Uhr).

steps.title: The weather and the seasons
steps.body: Weather is the safest small talk in Germany, especially on a Monday morning. Most weather sentences start with es: Es regnet, Es ist kalt.
steps.note: 'In Amman sind es heute dreißig Grad' gets a reaction from a German in November every single time.

steps.title: und, aber, oder: joining two sentences
steps.body: und (and), aber (but) and oder (or) join two sentences without changing anything. They stand outside the sentence, so what follows has its normal order: something in position one, then the verb. This is the easy one: Arabic wa and English 'and' work the same way. Put a comma before aber; before und and oder you usually don't. (Later you will meet weil and dass, which do change the order. These three never do.)

examples.de: Ich mag Berlin, aber es ist kalt.
examples.en: I like Berlin, but it's cold.

examples.de: Ich jogge und Mira schwimmt.
examples.en: I go jogging and Mira swims.

examples.de: Gehen wir ins Kino oder bleiben wir zu Hause?
examples.en: Shall we go to the cinema or stay at home?

examples.de: Im Sommer ist es heiß, aber im Winter regnet es.
examples.en: In summer it's hot, but in winter it rains.
examples.note: after aber, im Winter takes position one and the verb comes next

steps.question: Which sentence is correct?
options: Ich mag Sport, aber jogge ich nicht gern.
Ich mag Sport, aber ich jogge nicht gern.
Ich mag Sport aber, ich jogge nicht gern.
steps.why: aber does not move anything: after it comes ich, then the verb, as usual. And the comma goes before aber, not after it.

steps.title: Amman and Jordan
steps.body: Germans know Petra and the Dead Sea. Being able to tell them a little more about home is one of the nicest conversations you will have in German.

items.en: Amman has a lot of hills.

steps.note: Wadi Rum is simply 'die Wüste Wadi Rum'.

steps.title: A chat about a trip to Jordan
steps.body: Mira, a friend from Berlin, is going to visit Jordan and writes to you. Read the chat: what you say about the weather, the food and a day trip.

lines.de: Hallo {{name}}! Ich fliege im Oktober nach Jordanien. Wie ist das Wetter da?
lines.en: Hi {{name}}! I'm flying to Jordan in October. What's the weather like there?

lines.de: Im Oktober ist es warm, so fünfundzwanzig Grad. Es regnet fast nie.
lines.en: In October it's warm, about twenty-five degrees. It almost never rains.

lines.de: Super! Und was isst man in Amman?
lines.en: Great! And what do people eat in Amman?

lines.de: Am Freitag essen wir oft Mansaf. Das musst du probieren!
lines.en: On Fridays we often eat mansaf. You have to try it!

lines.de: Und was kann ich am Wochenende machen?
lines.en: And what can I do at the weekend?

lines.de: Das Tote Meer ist nicht weit, nur eine Stunde. Petra ist sehr schön, aber weit.
lines.en: The Dead Sea isn't far, only an hour. Petra is very beautiful, but far.

steps.question: What is the weather like in Amman in October?
options: Hot, and it rains a lot.
Warm, about 25 degrees, almost no rain.
Cold, and it rains often.
steps.why: 'Es ist warm, so fünfundzwanzig Grad. Es regnet fast nie.' fast nie means almost never, and 'so' before a number means about.

steps.question: Which place is far from Amman?
options: Petra
The Dead Sea
The old town
steps.why: 'Petra ist sehr schön, aber weit.' The Dead Sea is only an hour away: nicht weit, nur eine Stunde.

a1.2-2.outro: Now talk about your free time: open Talk and pick 'Montagmorgen'. Say what you like doing with gern, and ask back: 'Und du? Was machst du gern?'

a1.2-3.title: Das war gestern
a1.2-3.intro: Talking about the past: yesterday, last week, the weekend. After this lesson you can give a standup update (what you did, what you are doing, what is blocking you) and explain in simple words why a task is late.

student.intro: Talking about the past: yesterday, last week, the weekend. After this lesson you can tell your project group what you did, what you are doing and what the problem is, and explain in simple words why a report is late.
student.outro: Now tell your group what you did: open Talk and pick 'Projekttreffen: gestern, heute, Probleme'. Start with 'Gestern habe ich …' and put the participle at the end.

steps.title: war and hatte: was and had
steps.body: For 'was' and 'had', Germans don't build a long past form. They use two short words: war (from sein) and hatte (from haben). As with the modal verbs, ich and er / sie have the same form. 'Wie war dein Wochenende?' is the question you will hear every Monday, so this comes first.

examples.de: Wie war dein Wochenende?
examples.en: How was your weekend?

examples.de: Das Wetter war super.
examples.en: The weather was great.

examples.de: Ich hatte keine Zeit.
examples.en: I didn't have time.

examples.de: Gestern war ich krank.
examples.en: Yesterday I was ill.

examples.de: Wir hatten viel Arbeit.
examples.en: We had a lot of work.

steps.note: 'Ich bin gewesen' and 'ich habe gehabt' exist, but in everyday speech people simply say war and hatte.

steps.question: Someone asks you: 'Wie war dein Wochenende?' Which answer fits?
options: Es ist super.
Es war super.
Es hatte super.
steps.why: The weekend is over, so: war. 'Es ist super' talks about now, and hatte means 'had': Ich hatte Zeit.

steps.title: The Perfekt with haben
steps.body: For almost everything else in the past, spoken German uses the Perfekt: haben in position two and a participle at the very end. Regular verbs build it as ge- + stem + -t: machen → gemacht. A stem ending in -t or -d adds -et: testen → getestet. English has one word (I tested); German always has two, and the second one waits until the end.

examples.de: Ich habe gestern lange gearbeitet.
examples.en: I worked late yesterday.

examples.de: Hast du das schon getestet?
examples.en: Have you tested that yet?

examples.de: Wir haben am Samstag gekocht.
examples.en: We cooked on Saturday.

examples.de: Mira hat den Link geschickt.
examples.en: Mira sent the link.

steps.note: Verbs that are not stressed on the first syllable take no ge-: installieren → installiert, besprechen → besprochen.

steps.question: Which sentence is a correct Perfekt?
options: Ich habe die Aufgabe gemacht.
Ich habe gemacht die Aufgabe.
Ich habe die Aufgabe macht.
steps.why: habe in position two, the participle gemacht at the very end, and the participle needs its ge-: gemacht, not macht.

steps.title: Work verbs, now and in the past
steps.body: Learn the verb and its participle as a pair, out loud. English tech verbs follow the German rules: fixen → gefixt. deployen is stressed on the second syllable, so like installieren it takes no ge-.

items.en: to do, to make – done, made

student.title: Study verbs, now and in the past
student.body: Learn the verb and its participle as a pair, out loud. Verbs that are not stressed on the first syllable take no ge-: konstruieren → konstruiert.

steps.title: The Perfekt with sein: moving and changing
steps.body: Some verbs use sein instead of haben: verbs of moving from A to B (gehen, fahren, kommen, fliegen) and of changing state (aufstehen, einschlafen). bleiben belongs here too. Ask yourself: did I move or change? Then it is sein. Neither Arabic nor English makes this split, so learn 'ich bin gegangen' as one block. Most of these participles end in -en.

examples.de: Ich bin um sieben aufgestanden.
examples.en: I got up at seven.

examples.de: Wir sind nach Aqaba gefahren.
examples.en: We went to Aqaba.

examples.de: Bist du gut nach Hause gekommen?
examples.en: Did you get home all right?

examples.de: Am Sonntag bin ich zu Hause geblieben.
examples.en: On Sunday I stayed at home.

steps.question: How do you say 'I flew to Berlin'?
options: Ich habe nach Berlin geflogen.
Ich bin nach Berlin gefliegt.
Ich bin nach Berlin geflogen.
steps.why: fliegen is movement from A to B, so it takes sein: ich bin. And it is irregular: geflogen, not gefliegt.

steps.title: The common irregular participles
steps.body: Irregular verbs build the participle with ge- + -en, and many change their vowel: sehen → gesehen, schreiben → geschrieben, finden → gefunden. At A1 there is no rule worth learning; the good news is that a couple of dozen verbs cover almost everything you say. Learn them in pairs and say them aloud: finden – gefunden.

examples.de: Ich habe den Fehler gefunden.
examples.en: I found the mistake.

examples.de: Hast du meine E-Mail gelesen?
examples.en: Have you read my email?

examples.de: Wir haben zusammen gegessen.
examples.en: We ate together.

examples.de: Ich habe mit Mira gesprochen.
examples.en: I talked to Mira.

examples.de: Hast du den Film gesehen?
examples.en: Have you seen the film?

steps.question: Fill the gap: 'Ich habe gestern zwei E-Mails ___.'
options: geschreibt
geschrieben
schreibt
steps.why: schreiben is irregular: geschrieben, with ie and -en. 'geschreibt' is the regular pattern on an irregular verb, the most common mistake of all at this stage.

steps.title: When it happened
steps.body: These go near the start of the sentence or right after the verb. Start with one and the verb still comes second: Gestern habe ich …

items.note: letzte Woche, letzten Monat, letztes Jahr: the ending follows the noun's gender

steps.title: Separable verbs in the Perfekt, and the end of the sentence
steps.body: The participle always goes to the very end, however long the sentence is: everything else sits between haben / sein and the participle. Separable verbs put ge- between the prefix and the verb: anfangen → angefangen, anrufen → angerufen, aufstehen → aufgestanden. It is still one word, written together.

examples.de: Ich habe gestern um acht angefangen.
examples.en: I started at eight yesterday.

examples.de: Hast du Frau Sommer angerufen?
examples.en: Did you call Ms Sommer?

examples.de: Der Zug ist pünktlich angekommen.
examples.en: The train arrived on time.

examples.de: Ich habe am Samstag eingekauft.
examples.en: I went shopping on Saturday.

steps.question: Which sentence is right?
options: Ich habe gestern Jonas angerufen.
Ich habe gestern Jonas geanrufen.
Ich habe angerufen gestern Jonas.
steps.why: The ge- goes inside the separable verb: an-ge-rufen. And the participle goes to the very end, after gestern and Jonas.

steps.title: The standup
steps.body: A standup has three questions: what did you do yesterday, what are you doing today, is anything blocking you? These chunks answer all three. German teams use 'der Blocker' just like English ones.

items.en: That will take a while yet.

student.title: The project meeting
student.body: A project meeting often starts with the same three questions: what did you do, what are you doing today, is there a problem? These chunks answer all three.

steps.title: A message to the manager
steps.body: Jonas writes to your manager, Frau Dr. Sommer, in the team chat: his task is late. Read what he did, what went wrong, and when it will be ready.

lines.de: Guten Morgen, Frau Sommer, das Ticket für den Login ist leider noch nicht fertig.
lines.en: Good morning, Ms Sommer, unfortunately the ticket for the login isn't finished yet.

lines.de: Am Montag habe ich den Code geschrieben und getestet.
lines.en: On Monday I wrote and tested the code.

lines.de: Am Dienstag habe ich dann einen Fehler gefunden. Das war leider kompliziert.
lines.en: Then on Tuesday I found a bug. Unfortunately that was complicated.

lines.de: Gestern hatte ich viele Meetings.
lines.en: Yesterday I had a lot of meetings.

lines.de: Heute fixe ich den Fehler. Das Ticket ist am Freitag fertig.
lines.en: Today I'm fixing the bug. The ticket will be ready on Friday.

lines.de: Viele Grüße, Jonas
lines.en: Best regards, Jonas

student.title: A message to the lab supervisor
student.body: Jonas, who is in your lab course, writes to the supervisor, Herr Dr. Krüger: his lab report is late. Read what he did, what went wrong, and when it will be ready.

lines.de: Guten Morgen, Herr Dr. Krüger, mein Laborbericht ist leider noch nicht fertig.
lines.en: Good morning, Dr Krüger, unfortunately my lab report isn't finished yet.

lines.de: Am Montag habe ich im Labor gemessen und die Daten geprüft.
lines.en: On Monday I took measurements in the lab and checked the data.

lines.de: Am Dienstag habe ich dann einen Fehler in der Rechnung gefunden. Das war leider kompliziert.
lines.en: Then on Tuesday I found a mistake in the calculation. Unfortunately that was complicated.

lines.de: Gestern hatte ich viele Vorlesungen.
lines.en: Yesterday I had a lot of lectures.

lines.de: Heute rechne ich alles noch einmal. Der Bericht ist am Freitag fertig.
lines.en: Today I'm doing all the calculations again. The report will be ready on Friday.

lines.de: Viele Grüße, Jonas
lines.en: Best regards, Jonas

steps.question: Why is Jonas late?
options: He was ill on Tuesday.
He found a bug on Tuesday and had a lot of meetings yesterday.
He hasn't started yet.
steps.why: 'Am Dienstag habe ich einen Fehler gefunden' and 'Gestern hatte ich viele Meetings.' He wrote and tested the code on Monday, so he did start.

options: He was ill on Tuesday.
He found a mistake in his calculation on Tuesday and had a lot of lectures yesterday.
He hasn't started yet.
student.why: 'Am Dienstag habe ich einen Fehler in der Rechnung gefunden' and 'Gestern hatte ich viele Vorlesungen.' He measured and checked the data on Monday, so he did start.

steps.question: When will it be ready?
options: On Friday
Today
On Monday
steps.why: 'Das Ticket ist am Freitag fertig.' The present tense often means the future in German. Today he is fixing the bug: Heute fixe ich den Fehler.

student.why: 'Der Bericht ist am Freitag fertig.' The present tense often means the future in German. Today he is doing the calculations again: Heute rechne ich alles noch einmal.

a1.2-3.outro: Now give your first standup in German: open Talk and pick 'Standup: gestern, heute, Blocker'. Start with 'Gestern habe ich …' and put the participle at the end.

a1.2-4.title: Unterwegs
a1.2-4.intro: Getting around: trains, buses, the U-Bahn and taxis. After this lesson you can buy a ticket, find your platform, understand that your train is late, and ask the way to your hotel.

steps.title: Train travel
steps.body: The words on every station board and in every announcement. Gleis is the one to listen for: it is the number of your platform.

items.note: on the app and the machine you will also see 'das Ticket'

steps.note: der Hauptbahnhof (Hbf) is the main station of a city. If you are unsure where to go, go there.

steps.title: mit dem Zug, mit der Bahn: how you travel
steps.body: To say how you travel, German uses mit and a small article you can learn as a fixed chunk for now: dem for der- and das-words, der for die-words. (This is the dative, which gets its own unit in A2.1.) The traps: 'mit den Zug' and 'mit Zug'. Walking does not take mit at all: zu Fuß.

examples.de: Ich fahre mit dem Zug nach Hamburg.
examples.en: I'm going to Hamburg by train.

examples.de: Fährst du mit dem Bus?
examples.en: Are you going by bus?

examples.de: Mit der U-Bahn dauert es zehn Minuten.
examples.en: By U-Bahn it takes ten minutes.

examples.de: Ich gehe zu Fuß.
examples.en: I'm walking.

steps.note: With nehmen there is no mit, just the accusative: Ich nehme den Bus. Wir nehmen ein Taxi.

steps.question: How do you say 'I'm going by bus'?
options: Ich fahre mit dem Bus.
Ich fahre mit den Bus.
Ich fahre mit Bus.
steps.why: der Bus is a der-word, so after mit it becomes dem: mit dem Bus. German never leaves the article out here.

steps.title: abfahren, ankommen, umsteigen: travel verbs that split
steps.body: Travel German is full of separable verbs: abfahren (leave), ankommen (arrive), einsteigen (get on), umsteigen (change trains), aussteigen (get off). In a normal sentence the prefix jumps to the very end: Der Zug fährt um zehn ab. With a modal verb the verb stays whole at the end: Ich muss in Köln umsteigen. In announcements, listen for the little word at the end: ab or an changes everything.

head: verb
present
with müssen
rows: Der Zug fährt um zehn ab.

examples.de: Der Zug fährt um zehn Uhr ab.
examples.en: The train leaves at ten.

examples.de: Wann kommen wir in Berlin an?
examples.en: When do we arrive in Berlin?

examples.de: Ich muss in Hannover umsteigen.
examples.en: I have to change trains in Hannover.

examples.de: Wo muss ich aussteigen?
examples.en: Where do I have to get off?

steps.question: The train arrives at three. Which sentence says that?
options: Der Zug ankommt um drei.
Der Zug kommt um drei an.
Der Zug kommt an um drei.
steps.why: kommt takes position two and the prefix an goes to the very end, after the time: Der Zug kommt um drei an.

steps.title: Bus, U-Bahn, taxi and the airport
steps.body: In a city you will mostly take the U-Bahn (underground) and the S-Bahn (suburban trains). One ticket usually covers bus, U-Bahn and S-Bahn.

items.note: all you need to say to a taxi driver

steps.title: Wie komme ich zum …? Asking the way
steps.body: The question for directions is a fixed chunk: Wie komme ich zum …? for der- and das-places, and zur … for die-places. zum is short for zu dem and zur for zu der: the dative again, so for now just learn the place together with its zum or zur. Cities and countries have no article and take nach: nach Berlin. Home is nach Hause.

examples.de: Wie komme ich zum Flughafen?
examples.en: How do I get to the airport?

examples.de: Entschuldigung, wie komme ich zur Haltestelle?
examples.en: Excuse me, how do I get to the stop?

examples.de: Wie komme ich zum Hotel Adler?
examples.en: How do I get to the Hotel Adler?

examples.de: Ich fahre morgen nach Berlin.
examples.en: I'm going to Berlin tomorrow.

steps.question: You're looking for the U-Bahn station (die U-Bahn-Station). What do you ask?
options: Wie komme ich zum U-Bahn-Station?
Wie komme ich nach U-Bahn-Station?
Wie komme ich zur U-Bahn-Station?
steps.why: die Station is a die-word, so it is zur. zum is for der- and das-words, and nach is for cities and countries.

steps.title: der erste, der zweite, der dritte: ordinal numbers
steps.body: First, second, third: up to 19 you add -te to the number (der zweite, der vierte), from 20 on -ste (der zwanzigste). Four are irregular and worth learning by heart: erste, dritte, siebte, achte. You need them for floors (im dritten Stock), dates (am ersten Mai) and 'the second stop'. After der / die / das the ending is -e; after im, am, zum and an der it is -en.

examples.de: Die Wohnung ist im dritten Stock.
examples.en: The flat is on the third floor.

examples.de: Der erste Zug fährt um sechs.
examples.en: The first train leaves at six.

examples.de: Steigen Sie an der zweiten Haltestelle aus.
examples.en: Get off at the second stop.

examples.de: Heute ist der erste Mai.
examples.en: Today is the first of May.

steps.note: Platforms use plain numbers: Gleis drei, Gleis neun. And der erste Stock is one floor up; the ground floor is das Erdgeschoss, as in British English.

steps.question: At the hotel, the receptionist says: 'Ihr Zimmer ist im vierten Stock.' Where is your room?
options: In room number four
On the fourth floor
On the fourteenth floor
steps.why: vierten is the ordinal of vier, and der Stock is the floor: im vierten Stock = on the fourth floor. Fourteenth would be vierzehnten.

steps.title: Times and durations
steps.body: dauern means 'to take' for time. Wie lange dauert …? is the question, Es dauert … the answer.

items.en: How long does the journey take?

items.note: you will hear circa in every delay announcement

steps.title: An announcement at the station
steps.body: You are on the platform at Berlin Hauptbahnhof, waiting for the train to Hamburg. Listen for two things: how late the train is, and which platform it leaves from now.

lines.de: Achtung an Gleis sieben: eine Information zum ICE nach Hamburg, Abfahrt zehn Uhr zwölf.
lines.en: Attention at platform seven: information about the ICE to Hamburg, departure 10:12.

lines.de: Der Zug hat heute circa dreißig Minuten Verspätung.
lines.en: The train is running about thirty minutes late today.

lines.de: Grund dafür ist eine Reparatur am Zug.
lines.en: The reason is a repair on the train.

lines.de: Der ICE fährt heute von Gleis neun ab.
lines.en: Today the ICE leaves from platform nine.

lines.de: Haben Sie in Hamburg einen Anschluss? Dann fragen Sie bitte unser Personal im Zug.
lines.en: Do you have a connection in Hamburg? Then please ask our staff on the train.

lines.de: Wir bitten um Entschuldigung.
lines.en: We apologise.

steps.question: How late is the train?
options: Thirteen minutes
About thirty minutes
Two hours
steps.why: 'circa dreißig Minuten Verspätung' — circa means about. dreißig is 30 and dreizehn is 13: listen for the -ßig at the end.

steps.question: Where does the train leave from now?
options: Platform nine
Platform seven
The information desk
steps.why: The announcement is made at platform seven, but 'Der ICE fährt heute von Gleis neun ab.' Platform changes happen a lot, so always listen for the second number.

steps.title: A message on your phone
steps.body: Your train app sends you a message about your trip from Frankfurt to Berlin. Read it: what has changed, and what do you do now?

lines.de: Ihre Reise heute: Frankfurt (Main) Hbf – Berlin Hbf
lines.en: Your trip today: Frankfurt (Main) central station – Berlin central station

lines.de: Ihr ICE hat circa 15 Minuten Verspätung. Neue Abfahrt: 9:45 Uhr.
lines.en: Your ICE is about 15 minutes late. New departure: 9:45.

lines.de: Ihren Anschluss in Hannover schaffen Sie leider nicht.
lines.en: Unfortunately you won't make your connection in Hannover.

lines.de: Neue Verbindung: Umsteigen in Hannover, Abfahrt 11:52 Uhr von Gleis 4.
lines.en: New connection: change in Hannover, departure 11:52 from platform 4.

lines.de: Ihre Fahrkarte gilt auch für diesen Zug. Ankunft in Berlin: 14:10 Uhr.
lines.en: Your ticket is also valid for this train. Arrival in Berlin: 14:10.

steps.question: What happens to your connection in Hannover?
options: You will make it: the train waits.
You will miss it and take a later train.
It is cancelled and you need a new ticket.
steps.why: 'schaffen Sie leider nicht' = you won't make it. Then comes the new connection at 11:52, and 'Ihre Fahrkarte gilt auch für diesen Zug': your ticket is valid, no new one needed.

steps.question: When do you arrive in Berlin?
steps.why: Ankunft means arrival: 14:10 Uhr. 9:45 is the new departure from Frankfurt (Abfahrt), and 11:52 is the train from Hannover.

a1.2-4.outro: Now try it out loud: open Talk and pick 'Am Fahrkartenautomaten'. Say where you want to go with 'Ich möchte nach … fahren', and if you get lost, 'Noch einmal, bitte' still works.

a1.2-5.title: Meine Wohnung
a1.2-5.intro: Your home: the rooms, the furniture, and the questions you ask about a flat to rent. After this lesson you can describe your flat in Amman, read a German flat ad, and ask a landlord about the size, the rent and the extra costs.

steps.title: Rooms and furniture
steps.body: Most rooms are das Zimmer with something in front: Wohnzimmer, Schlafzimmer, Arbeitszimmer. A compound always takes the gender of its last part, so they are all das.

steps.title: One room, two rooms: the plural
